back: [[kw:Statistics]] is the [[imp:science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data]] to make decisions.
It transforms raw data into [[imp:informed decisions]].
[[kw:Data]] are [[imp:information from observations, counts, measurements, or responses]].
They can be numbers (quantitative) or labels (qualitative).
A [[kw:population]] is the [[imp:complete collection]] of all items of interest.
Think “whole group” – e.g., all adults in the U.S.
A [[kw:sample]] is a [[imp:subset]] of a population.
We use samples because measuring an entire population is usually [[imp:impractical]].
A [[kw:census]] collects data from [[imp:every member]] of a population.
It's often too expensive or time‑consuming for large groups.
A [[kw:parameter]] is a [[imp:numerical description of a population]].
It's fixed (usually unknown). Memory tip: [[imp:P]]arameter ↔ [[imp:P]]opulation.
A [[kw:statistic]] is a [[imp:numerical description of a sample]].
It varies from sample to sample. Memory tip: [[imp:S]]tatistic ↔ [[imp:S]]ample.
A [[kw:statistic]] varies from sample to sample.
A [[kw:parameter]] is fixed but often unknown.
We use a sample [[kw:statistic]] to [[imp:estimate]] the unknown population [[kw:parameter]].
The statistic is our best guess for the parameter.
cards.front: How are a [[kw:statistic]] and a [[kw:parameter]] connected?

back: [[kw:Descriptive statistics]] [[imp:organizes, summarizes, and displays]] data.
Tools: charts, averages, percentages. It stays within the sample.
[[kw:Inferential statistics]] [[imp:uses a sample to draw conclusions]] about a population.
It relies on [[imp:probability]] to make inferences.
The [[kw:percentages]] (70% and 90%) are [[kw:descriptive]].
A possible [[kw:inferential]] conclusion: [[imp:Marriage is associated with longer life.]]
cards.front: 70% of unmarried men lived to 65 vs. 90% of married men. Which part is descriptive?
What must a sample be for valid conclusions?
back: [[imp:Representative]] of the population.
If a sample is [[imp:biased]], conclusions are unreliable.
[[kw:Qualitative data]]: [[imp:labels, attributes, or nonnumerical entries]] (e.g., car models).
[[kw:Quantitative data]]: [[imp:numerical measurements or counts]] (e.g., prices, heights).
Key test: can you do meaningful arithmetic?
cards.front: What is the difference between [[kw:qualitative data]] and [[kw:quantitative data]]?

back: Types of TV shows (comedy, drama, sports).
Jersey numbers (used as labels, not measurements).
Political party (Democrat, Republican, Independent).
[[imp:Even if numbers appear, they may be qualitative if they act as labels.]]
Weights of infants at a hospital.
Number of home runs hit by a team.
Lengths of songs on an MP3 player.
[[imp:These are numbers you can add, average, or compare meaningfully.]]
[[imp:Categorization only.]] No order, no meaningful differences.
Examples: types of shows, network call letters, eye colors.
Even numbers used as labels are nominal.
Data can be [[imp:arranged in order or ranked]], but differences are not meaningful.
Examples: TV show rankings, MPAA ratings (G, PG, PG‑13...), class rank.
The gap between ranks may not be equal.
Order and [[imp:meaningful differences]] are allowed.
[[imp:No true zero]] — zero is just a position on a scale.
Ratios don't make sense (e.g., 40°F isn't twice as hot as 20°F).
Has all properties of interval, plus a [[imp:true zero]] that means “none.”
Ratios are meaningful: $20 is twice $10.
Examples: prices, heights, weights, home run totals.

cards.front: How do you test whether data are interval or ratio?
back: Ask: “Does zero mean [[imp:complete absence]] of what I'm measuring?”
If yes → [[kw:ratio]]. If zero is just a point → [[kw:interval]].
Example: 0°F doesn't mean no heat (interval); $0 means no money (ratio).
[[kw:Nominal]] — categories only.
[[kw:Ordinal]] — categories + order.
[[kw:Interval]] — + meaningful differences, no true zero.
[[kw:Ratio]] — + true zero and ratios.
[[imp:Always assign the highest level that applies.]]
cards.front: What are the four levels of measurement in order?
Are jersey numbers qualitative or quantitative? What level?
back: [[kw:Qualitative]] — they are [[imp:labels]], not measurements.
Adding them gives meaningless results.
Level: [[kw:nominal]].
They can be ordered, but differences aren't measurable viewer counts.
Level: [[kw:ordinal]].
[[kw:Quantitative]]. Can be ordered, differences meaningful.
0°F is not absolute zero heat.
Level: [[kw:interval]].
[[kw:Quantitative]].
True zero (0 lbs = no weight), ratios meaningful.
Level: [[kw:ratio]].
cards.front: Classify the weight of an athlete.
What are the four main methods of [[kw:data collection]]?
back: 1. [[kw:Observational study]] – observe without interfering.
2. [[kw:Experiment]] – apply a treatment, compare results.
3. [[kw:Simulation]] – use a model to imitate reality.
4. [[kw:Survey]] – ask questions to a sample.
Researcher [[imp:observes and measures characteristics]] without influencing.
No treatment is applied.
Example: recording children's mouthing behavior.
A [[imp:treatment is applied]] and responses compared to a [[imp:control group]].
Control group may receive a [[kw:placebo]].
Example: testing a new allergy drug.
A [[imp:mathematical or physical model]] reproduces a real‑world situation.
Used when actual study is [[imp:impractical or dangerous]].
Example: crash test dummies.
Collects data by [[imp:asking questions]] to a sample.
Can be interview, mail, or phone. [[imp:Wording must be neutral.]]

cards.front: What are the three key elements of experimental design?
back: 1. [[kw:Control]] – limit outside variables; use a control group.
2. [[kw:Randomization]] – randomly assign subjects to groups.
3. [[kw:Replication]] – use a large enough sample to verify results.
An outside factor that [[imp:makes it impossible to tell]] which variable caused the effect.
Example: coffee shop remodel + new mall opening simultaneously.
[[kw:Blinding]]: subjects don't know if they receive treatment or placebo.
[[kw:Double‑blind]]: [[imp:neither subjects nor experimenters know]] until data collection ends.
Both reduce [[imp:placebo effect]] and bias.
Every member has an [[imp:equal chance]] of being selected.
Every possible sample of that size is equally likely.
Uses random number tables or generators.
Divide population into subgroups ([[kw:strata]]) sharing a characteristic.
Take a [[imp:random sample from each stratum]].
Ensures representation across groups.
Divide population into clusters (e.g., zip codes).
Randomly select whole clusters and [[imp:include all members]] in those clusters.
Clusters should be similar to each other.
Random start, then select every k‑th member.
Easy to use, but [[imp:avoid if data have a pattern]].
Example: testing every 50th light bulb.
Selects [[imp:easily available]] subjects.
[[imp:High risk of bias]]; not representative.
Example: surveying only people walking by a booth.
Subjects grouped by a characteristic ([[kw:block]]), e.g., age, gender.
[[imp:Within each block, randomly assign]] to treatments.
Controls for the blocking variable.
Subjects are [[imp:paired based on similarity]] (twins, or same person before/after).
One gets treatment A, the other B.
Reduces variability due to individual differences.
